2a(1).fact: Clay bodies for sculpture require coarse additives like grog to reduce shrinkage, prevent cracking, and support thick walls that would otherwise collapse.
2a(1).misconception: Smooth clay bodies with high plasticity are better suited for large sculptures than gritty clay bodies containing grog.
2a(1).pamphlet_summary: Clay bodies formulated for hand-building sculptures incorporate grog or coarse sand to provide structural tooth, minimize warping, and decrease shrinkage during drying. These additives allow artisans to construct thick or uneven sculptural walls without sagging or cracking before firing (p. 18).
2a(1).socratic_question: What structural problems would happen if you tried to hand-build a heavy, thick-walled sculpture out of silky, fine-grained porcelain?

2a(2).fact: Throwing clay bodies prioritize fine-grained plasticity and minimal coarse aggregate to allow smooth pulling without abrading the potter's palms at high speeds.
2a(2).misconception: Coarse grog should be added generously to wheel clay to give the potter extra grip while pulling up walls.
2a(2).pamphlet_summary: Wheel-throwing clay formulations require high plasticity and fine particle distribution to allow potters to center and pull tall walls without tearing. These bodies contain balanced moisture and minimal coarse aggregate to withstand centrifugal force while remaining gentle on the hands during spinning (p. 21).
2a(2).socratic_question: What happens to your hands and the clay walls if you try to center and pull a vessel on a spinning wheel using coarse, gritty clay?
